format:
  html:
    code-fold: true

```{r}
#| label: setup
# install.packages(c("readxl","dplyr","ggplot2","sf","giscoR","scales","ggrepel","stringr"))
library(readxl); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2); library(sf)
library(giscoR); library(scales); library(ggrepel); library(stringr)

# Excel file lives in the data/ folder
f <- "data/destatis_21311-0002_clean.xlsx"

state_en <- c(BW="Baden-Württemberg", BY="Bavaria", BE="Berlin", BB="Brandenburg",
              HB="Bremen", HH="Hamburg", HE="Hesse", MV="Mecklenburg-Vorpommern",
              NI="Lower Saxony", NW="North Rhine-Westphalia", RP="Rhineland-Palatinate",
              SL="Saarland", SN="Saxony", ST="Saxony-Anhalt",
              SH="Schleswig-Holstein", TH="Thuringia")

# NUTS1 codes for the 16 Länder (used to join the map geometry)
nuts <- c(BW="DE1", BY="DE2", BE="DE3", BB="DE4", HB="DE5", HH="DE6", HE="DE7",
          MV="DE8", NI="DE9", NW="DEA", RP="DEB", SL="DEC", SN="DED", ST="DEE",
          SH="DEF", TH="DEG")

st <- read_excel(f, sheet = "States") |>
  filter(!is.na(`State code`)) |>
  transmute(code = `State code`, state = state_en[`State code`],
            foreign = `Foreign students`, total = `All students`,
            share = `Foreign share (%)`,
            share_excl_distance = `Foreign share excl. distance providers (%)`)

inst_all <- read_excel(f, sheet = "Institutions") |>
  transmute(name = `Institution / campus (as in Destatis)`,
            code = `State code`,
            type = `Institution type (my classification)`,
            distance = `Distance-learning provider (my classification)`,
            foreign = `Foreign total`, total = `All students`,
            share = `Foreign share (%)`)

inst <- filter(inst_all, total >= 1000)          # avoids tiny-denominator extremes
nat  <- sum(st$foreign) / sum(st$total) * 100    # national share, ~18.0 %
```

## The question

Germany had **`r format(sum(st$foreign), big.mark = ",")`** students with foreign
nationality in WS 2025/26, **`r round(nat, 1)`%** of all students. But how evenly
are they spread across states and institutions?

## 1. The map: a range from 10.8% to 27.8%

```{r}
#| label: fig-map
#| fig-cap: "Share of students with foreign nationality by federal state, WS 2025/26. Source: Destatis 21311-0002; own calculation."
geo <- gisco_get_nuts(year = "2021", nuts_level = 1, country = "DE", resolution = "10") |>
  left_join(mutate(st, NUTS_ID = nuts[code]), by = "NUTS_ID")

ggplot(geo) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = share), colour = "white", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = paste0(round(share, 1), "%")), size = 3, colour = "white",
               fontface = "bold", check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "% foreign\nnationality", option = "mako",
                       direction = -1, end = .9) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

**How to read it.** The share of students with foreign nationality ranges from 10.8% in Schleswig-Holstein to 27.8% in Brandenburg, with Germany overall at 18.0%. Berlin (25.9%) and Bavaria (22.1%) are also well above average, while Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (11.5%) and Baden-Württemberg (14.7%) are below it. The map shows where the share is high or low, not why.

## 2. Share versus absolute numbers

Large states have many international students simply because they have many
students overall. Share and count answer different questions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-states
#| fig-cap: "Left: share of students with foreign nationality. Right: number of students. Dashed line: national share."
#| fig-height: 6
st_long <- st |>
  mutate(state = reorder(state, share)) |>
  transmute(state, `Share of students (%)` = share, `Students with foreign nationality` = foreign) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-state)

ggplot(st_long, aes(value, state, fill = name)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#c2410c", "#0b6e6e")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

**How to read it.** Share and size give different rankings. North Rhine-Westphalia has the most students with foreign nationality (113,075) but only 15.9% of its students, because it has so many students overall. Brandenburg has just 15,685 but the highest share. The left panel shows how concentrated a state's student body is; the right panel shows how many students are involved.

## 3. Institutions vary more than states

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Institutions and campuses with at least 1,000 students. Point size = number of students with foreign nationality."
labs_df <- inst |>
  filter(str_detect(name, "Technische Hochschule Aachen|Garching|Gisma|Fernuniversität Hagen|IU Int. H Erfurt in Erfurt|Constructor|Rhein-Waal in Kleve")) |>
  mutate(label = str_trunc(name, 28))

ggplot(inst, aes(total, share, size = foreign)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .4, colour = "#0b6e6e") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nat, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c2410c") +
  annotate("text", x = 1e5, y = nat + 3, label = paste0("Germany ", round(nat, 1), "%"),
           colour = "#c2410c", hjust = 1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_text_repel(data = labs_df, aes(label = label), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 9, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "All students at the institution (log scale)",
       y = "% with foreign nationality") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**How to read it.** Each dot is an institution or campus with at least 1,000 students. Shares span 0% to 99%, with a median of 14% and the middle 80% between 3.7% and 35.7%, a far wider spread than between states. The extremes are mostly small, specialised or international-by-design institutions. Large technical universities (RWTH Aachen 35.7%, TU Munich Garching 45.7%) combine size with high shares.

## 4. Two rankings, two different lists

```{r}
#| label: fig-rank
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 institutions by share (left, at least 1,000 students) and by number (right)."
#| fig-height: 5
top_share <- inst |> slice_max(share, n = 10) |> mutate(rank = "Highest share (%)", value = share)
top_n     <- inst |> slice_max(foreign, n = 10) |> mutate(rank = "Most students with foreign nationality", value = foreign)

bind_rows(top_share, top_n) |>
  mutate(name = str_trunc(name, 38), name = tidytext::reorder_within(name, value, rank)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, name, fill = rank)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  tidytext::scale_y_reordered() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0b6e6e", "#c2410c")) +
  facet_wrap(~rank, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

**How to read it.** The two lists barely overlap. The highest shares belong to small institutions such as Gisma and the University of Europe in Potsdam (about 99%), Constructor University Bremen (95%) and the Deggendorf Rottal-Inn campus (97.5%). The highest numbers belong to large institutions: IU Erfurt (16,595), RWTH Aachen (15,939), TU Berlin (10,424) and TU Munich Garching (10,288). A ranking by share alone says little about how many students are affected.

## Sensitivity: distance-learning providers

IU Internationale Hochschule (a distance provider registered in Erfurt, 108,463
students) pulls Thuringia's share down. Excluding distance providers:

```{r}
#| label: fig-distance
#| fig-cap: "State shares with and without distance-learning providers (my classification)."
st |>
  mutate(state = reorder(state, share)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = state)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = share, xend = share_excl_distance, yend = state), colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(x = share), colour = "grey40", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = share_excl_distance), colour = "#0b6e6e", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "% foreign nationality (grey: all, teal: excl. distance providers)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**How to read it.** Distance providers can shift a state's share noticeably. IU Internationale Hochschule, registered in Erfurt, has 108,463 students, and its share of foreign students is below average. Excluding distance providers, Thuringia rises from 17.4% to 22.1%, Bremen from 22.1% to 24.6%, and the national share from 18.0% to 18.5%. The story should state which version it uses.

## Caveats

- Nationality only: the table does not separate students who obtained their
  entrance qualification abroad (Bildungsausländer).
- State is not in the source file; it was assigned from the file's row order
  and should be checked against table 21311-0005.
- Rows are campuses, not whole universities.
- Single semester (WS 2025/26): no time trend without further tables.

*Source: Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis), table 21311-0002, retrieved
05.11.2026. © Destatis, 2026.*
